**No. And this one is not a close call.**

Eliza said it herself in the Q4 plan review: *"If our brand has to bid on the word 'gift' in December, we did the first ten months wrong."* That quote is logged as the hard on Saltline's Q4 media plan. Leo budgeted accordingly at the time.

Three layers are working against this:

- **The client said no, explicitly.** Eliza blocked paid against the gift guide in the Q4 review. This is her brand position, not a preference we can work around.
- **Our own standard blocks it.** No paid creative ships until the message has a 14-day organic window. There's no record of that window being opened on holiday gift guide copy.

**The recommendation:** Hold paid. If Leo wants December traction for Saltline, the play is organic shoulder-season storytelling tied to how people actually cook and gift in winter — not bidding on "gift" in a crowded December auction.

Eliza's position on this is unusually clear, and consistent across every interaction we have on record.

**The core principle:** Voice over the window. Every time.

Her exact words from the kickoff, twelve minutes in: *"I would rather miss a launch window than ship a campaign that smells like everyone else's brand."* She said it without flinching. We have that quote in multiple forms across notes, voice memos, and follow-ups — and it has never been walked back.

**This is structural, not situational.** We noted it explicitly: "Eliza will miss a window before drifting voice — observed twice now. Not a negotiation tactic; a structural preference." She deferred the shoulder-season launch by a week when concerns came up, and agreed without a fight. She also said she would rather lose a holiday window than have Saltline sound like a wellness app. Category sameness is the enemy, not the calendar.

**What this means operationally:**

- She will block a launch over a single word in a subject line — budget the revision cycle accordingly
- Drafts go to her on Thursday mornings so she can do her kitchen read and clear approvals within 24 hours
- No paid spend against the holiday gift guide, full stop — *"If our brand has to bid on 'gift' in December, we did the first ten months wrong"*
- Ops (Theo's side) gates thecalendar too, so warehouse capacity is a secondary she respects

**The short version:** Never present a deadline as the reason to ship something that isn't right. She will choose the slip every time. Build that into every launch plan for Saltline.

agentRun.finalAnswer:
Wendell's test is the **Bloomberg Headline Survival Rule**:

> *"If your headline survives a Bloomberg headline cycle, it is ours. If it sounds like a Series A press release, it is not."*

In practice that means one filter: could this headline run in a Bloomberg article without looking out of place? If yes, it passes. If it reads like startup launch copy, it's dead on arrival.

Sara cites this rule in every Helmsmark copy review. It pairs with the second kill condition Wendell enforced directly — he pulled "AI-powered" from the hero himself, on the grounds that no CFO has ever wired money because something was AI-powered. The replacement line cited the variance number because that is what finance buyers actually respond to.

The two-part standard in plain terms:
- **Sounds like Bloomberg** (sober, specific, defensible)
- **Not a Series A press release** (no launch hype, no tech adjectives, no "we're disrupting" framing)

Crystal clear from everything we've logged on Dominic. Here's exactly what he wants:

## Dominic's Content Format: Forwardable Looms

**The one format he will accept:** Short Loom videos that a COO would forward to their CEO.

His exact words from the media plan review:
> *"My buyers do not read white papers. They forward Loom videos to their CEO and we either show up in those Looms or we do not."*

### What this means in practice:

- **Video-first, not written.** White papers, thought leadership articles, content hubs — all killed on the spot.
- **Forward-worthy, not just viewable.** The test is: would a COO peer forward this at a breakfast meeting? If not, it doesn't ship.
- **Operator language, not marketing language.** He rejected partnership-driven positioning and anything that reads like six firms in a trench coat.
- **Low volume, high signal.** Same philosophy on outbound — three a week, not three hundred. Content follows the same logic.

### What gets him to say no immediately:

- Top-of-funnel content blitzes (shut down in kickoff)
- SDR sequences before positioning is locked
- Templates that could apply to any COO
- Thought leadership for its own sake

The homepage passed his "forward test" because Aliyah line-edited it to match breakfast conversation truth. That's the bar for every content piece: would Dominic forward it to one of the four COOs he has standing breakfasts with?

**Bottom line:** One well-crafted Loom beats a hundred pieces of written content for this client.

**The core principle**
> "Our cohort is twenty-eight adults who took two hours out of a Tuesday. The course page has to honor that, not impress them."

The short version: treat cohort members as people who gave real time to be there, and write the page as if you owe them clarity — not as if you're still trying to close them.

Based on everything we know about Plinthworks, here is the gate sequence before any marketing post ships:

**1. Docs come first**
Self-serve flow docs must be updated before the launch post. Devi enforces this sequence — docs before hero, every time.

**2. Two engineers sign off on every technical claim**
Devi's hard rule: no marketing post ships until two engineers on her team have nodded at the technical claim. Marcus is the named checkpoint. This is not a courtesy review — she will not publish without it.

**3. Numbers must be verified against internal dashboards**
Any benchmark, latency stat, or performance claim in the post must match what's on the internal dashboard. Devi will not put a single number on the marketing site she cannot defend in a customer call.

**4. The internal upvote test**
The editorial policy (by acclamation after Marcus echoed it): "If we ship a launch post our platform team would not upvote internally, we should not ship it externally." If engineers wouldn't read it, it doesn't ship.

**5. Organic before paid**
If the post is tied to any paid amplification, the organic version must clear a pipeline threshold first. Devi killed Leo's paid test plan with exactly this logic. The PR merges before the paid test, not after.

**6. On-call hero mentions need dual sign-off**
Any on-call channel reference in a hero or hero-adjacent asset requires both Devi and Marcus to sign off.

The short version: docs are live, two engineers have cleared every technical claim, all numbers are verified, and the internal team would actually read it. That is the bar.

Based on what Foundry's brain has logged across multiple client threads: **month three, not month one.**

Sara named it explicitly in Week 10 — and it's been reinforced across Plinthworks, Helmsmark, Cloverkin, and Almanac retainers. The pattern is consistent.

**Why month three?**

The root cause is the SOW shape. Every Foundry SOW is sold as a retainer but written like a project — monthly deliverable line items instead of operating loop language. That tension stays quiet in the early weeks because there's enough new-engagement energy to paper over it.

Around day 60, it surfaces:

- The client asks for the next milestone deliverable (because that's what the SOW enumerated)
- Foundry wants to shift into the operating loop conversation
- Neither side is wrong — they just signed two different mental contracts

Plinthworks hit it at day 62. Helmsmark's CFO read the SOW as an hourly project by week 8. Saltline had the kitchenware ask at week 10.

**What Foundry is doing about it:**

Owen is drafting a v2 retainer SOW (Week 13) that closes the language gap. The goal is to replace deliverable line items with operating loop language before the contract is signed — so both sides enter month three with the same expectations.

One signal worth watching: this is still logged as a belief in the cortex, not studio law. Sara pushed back on it for Plinthworks and Cloverkin. Worth a partner sync conversation to lock it as a hard operating principle if the v2 SOW confirms the pattern.
